utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Before I call for the appearances for today, I note for the record that, today, and for the duration of this week, we'll be sitting under the provisions of Rule 15 bis; Judge Delvoie being absent. And speaking of the rest of this week, when we adjourned on Thursday, I indicated that for this week we would be sitting in the afternoons. I suppose everyone now would have seen the updated calendar and would appreciate that for the remainder of this week we are scheduled to sit in the mornings in Courtroom III. Yes, may have I the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, assisted by case manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Erin Dunnavant, and Stephanie Cagnet for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the Prosecution ready to have its witness take the stand? There are any matters that -- Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I notified the usher and the Registrar that I have two preliminary matters, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will -- I will make the -- the first -- the first submission in Serbian, in order to be clearly on the record. [Interpretation] Your Honours, a while ago, we discussed the issue and the topic that I would like to inform the Trial Chamber about, and at that time you suggested that the parties in the proceedings should try and seek a solution and agreement on the issue by themselves. We had expected this problem to have been overcome; however, on Thursday, we received information from the Prosecution in a letter sent by Ms. Korner that this problem is still outstanding. The issue is the objection on the part of the Prosecution for the Defence to be -- to interview the witnesses upon their arrival in The Hague. The Prosecution claims that this practice allegedly contributes to the witness's being nervous and under pressure, and that for that reason they allegedly give answers and different evidence from those contained in their statement, and that thereby they are not assisting the Trial Chamber or, according to the Prosecution, is such practice in the interests of justice. The Defence, however, asserts that nothing of the above is true. That is to say that our interviews with the witnesses who agree to be interviewed by the Defence, does not create any nervousness with the witnesses. Quite the contrary. The witnesses do not feel to be under any pressure whatsoever. Quite the contrary. And their evidence is the result of the fact that the Defence puts questions to them and show them documents that the Prosecution, for some reason, had omitted to show them or to ask them specific questions. I'm not going to go now into the reasons why the Prosecution omits to ask questions that pop up quite naturally or why the Prosecution fails to show to the witnesses all the relevant documents that this particular witness can provide a comment or an explanation. We maintain firmly that these interviews conducted by the Defence with the Prosecution witnesses will primarily be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in that it will get a fuller picture about the facts and ultimately about the witness himself, and that -- that is in the best possible interests of justice because the objective is to elicit from a witness full answers about relevant facts, not only about the selected facts that suit or corroborate the views of one of the parties or their case theory. We also believe that the Defence has the right to interview Prosecution witnesses at the time and in the place that is the most practical both for the witness and the Defence. This attitude of ours has been supported by the case law of this Tribunal. For reference, I am -- will take the ruling of the Appeals Chamber in the case against Sefer Halilovic, dated the 21st of June, 2004, paragraph 12, which reads and I'm quoting: [In English] "Where a witness is listed by one party as expected to testify on its behalf with respect to certain issues, it does not necessarily follow that this witness will have no information of value to the opposing party on other issues related to the case. The opposing party may have a legitimate expectation of interviewing such witness in order to obtain this information and thereby better prepare a case for its client. To deprive this expecting party of such ability would hand an unfair advantage to the opposing party which would be able to block its opponent's ability to interview crucial witnesses simply by placing them on its witness list." [Interpretation] I think that this ruling of the Appeals Chamber completely supports the views proffered here by the Defence, both in our previous submission and our today's submission. I have to say, Your Honours, admittedly the Prosecution does not object to interviewing the witnesses in principle, but it denies or objects to the right of the Defence to exercising this right in The Hague upon the arrival of the witnesses and prior to their testimony. We have serious issues with these objections, and we claim that the views of the witness does not change, but is rather supplemented by being asked the questions to the witness which obviously are essential, and by the fact that relevant documents are shown to the witness. Our fact is that when the Defence is interviewing the witness, whether it be a month, a week, or three days before the testimony, bears no effect on a witness's evidence. You will recall, Your Honours, that the Defence did not interview the last five Prosecution witnesses. Three of the five have changed their evidence, and they explained to the Chamber that in the course of their testimony, for the first time, they had an opportunity to see certain documents that hadn't been shown to them beforehand that it helped them to refresh the memory about the events that they were giving testimony about. In conclusion, Your Honours, you are aware of our situation with regard to the resources and manpower at the disposal of the Defence, and I'm not going to repeat that. The Prosecution also knows that we are using every adjournment to travel to the field and interview the witnesses. But also the fact is that the adjournments often coincide with holidays, and in such situations, the witnesses do not find it suitable or other reasons quoted for them to meet with the Defence. This case happened in January, for example, when, due to the fact that the roads were impassable, I had to postpone my trip to Bosnia and the interviews that I had agreed and arranged with three witnesses. The same happened during the Easter breaks, when, of the three witnesses that hi arranged interviews with I managed to interview only one. I would particularly like to underline that according to the statistics of 55 witnesses, that today's witness is the 55th. That is to say, of the 54 witnesses that appeared so far, the Defence interviewed only 18 of them, which is slightly below 30 per cent, which I believe is quite reasonable and justified. And now, Your Honours, we believe that it is in the best interest, from the aspect of time and cost-saving, that we continue with this practice. That is to say that the Defence be allowed to conduct an interview of a couple of hours with the witnesses upon their arrival in The Hague because it will cut the costs. Because, first of all, all witnesses are coming here just to testify. They have no other commitments. Secondly, the Defence can present to them hard copies of all documents available in The Hague, and thereby it will enable these witnesses to read them in full and to analyse them completely. Your Honours, this is the problem that we are facing at the moment. I apologise for taking some time, but I thought it was necessary for me to shed light on this problem because we already have a problem with regard to the next witness, because the Prosecution is opposed to our interviewing him here in The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the -- apart from the record in this trial now having the benefit of your considered views on this subject which we thought had been resolved to the extent that the Chamber is capable of resolving it as a matter of basic principle, do I understand when you say the next witness, the witness that is scheduled for this week, that there is a particular problem that you have in respect of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I meant the witness after the witness that is to appear today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, I'm sure that you have no -- you don't resist any of the general principles articulated by Mr. Zecevic. But in terms of what I understand his immediate complaint to be, that is, to the facilitation of the witness that is next on your list, I assume that as the Chamber has indicated previously that this is something that counsel could work out on the ground, in consultation with the Registry between themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, firstly, I'm glad that Mr. Zecevic started -- well, he started by reading out the judgement in Halilovic, did make it clear that there is no question of us saying that you cannot interview the witnesses whom we are about do call; it's the timing. And I'm sorry that it has to come up again, Your Honours. Your Honours, did -- I believe, Judge Delvoie invited to power water, not oil, on it. And we have tried to arrive at a solution, but it is just not possible. Our objection as summarised perfectly adequately by Mr. Zecevic is that the witnesses are not seen until the day before or the same day, as has happened today, the witness was seen again this morning by Mr. Zecevic. And then we were given an opportunity to deal with some rather important matters that came up last time. It is the timing that we really think is not assisting Your Honours to see what the witnesses might be saying if they weren't under what, I think anybody would agree, is pressure. And thereby, the -- we say the interests of justice are being affected. Can I say just briefly, in respect of this, to show that -- this is -- I don't want to say it's a deliberate ploy, but it is clearly something that may concern Your Honours. Mr. Zecevic - I'm not sure whether Mr. Pantelic - wrote to us in October of 2008 and said that he wished to interview some 33 witnesses who were then on the witness list. That was before the joinder. Indeed, before I came into the case at all. He was given the details of those who were prepared to speak to him. The majority of those witnesses were on the list in October and have remained on the list. No attempt, as we understand it, because we weren't informed of it, was made to contact any of those witnesses between October 2008 and October 2009. When we were asked for a much longer list, because the witnesses had changed because of Zupljanin, and again we gave the details of those who were prepared to speak to the Defence. No attempt whatsoever was made by the Stanisic Defence to get in touch with these witnesses as far as we know because we have to be informed by the terms Your Honours' ruling. In each and every case, they wait until the witness is due to testify. Your Honours, the explanation for that, and I accept, is that they don't employ an investigator. But they employ lawyers instead. And if that's their decision, well, then a lawyer can go and interview these witnesses. As far as the last five witnesses are concerned -- can I go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we revert to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll simply repeat what I said a moment ago. It is -- as I say, it doesn't sake rocket science to see that these witnesses are making sometimes dramatic alterations from what they have said originally either in interviews with the OTP or indeed in testimony. And today's witness is -- is one. And Your Honours will have to go through the three changes that he -- he's made to his original testimony. Your Honours, the other added matter is that it really is pressure for witnesses to be sat down by the OTP and asked to go through a number of documents and then either before or after to have to do the same with the Defence. We say the Defence can split their resources if they want to, can send out Mr. Zupljanin's two or three investigators to -- to see these people on behalf of both defendants. But we say that it is a proper thing for us to object to, is this bringing them up and then turning them over to the Defence just before they testify. And, Your Honours, the only reason we have raised it is we cannot agree on this. It is our view that it is contrary to the interests of justice. The Defence dispute that. And it's a matter we are going to ask Your Honours to rule on. If Your Honours order us as far as -- I don't know that you can actually order us to do it. But, nonetheless, if you make it clear that you expect us to continue with this practice of bringing witnesses up in advance sufficient for the Defence to see them, despite the submissions we have made, then we'll continue to do it. Our view is that this can be down either by a lawyer or an investigator in advance of -- of testimony, at least a week in advance. Because the Defence know well in advance who we will be calling, subject to changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, that you put your finger on the problem that, as I perceive it to be, that is the -- what the Chamber is empowered to order. And like any court anywhere, we have no intention of acting in vein. And we aren't going to purport to do something that we have no power to enforce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm saying, even if you don't actually have the power -- and under, I think it's Rule 54, you have the power to regulate virtually everything that comes before the Court. If you make it clear that despite what we have said, that you think there is merit in what Mr. Zecevic has argued, then regardless of our view that we think that this is not a proper way of dealing with it, we will continue to call the witnesses here in advance, subject to, you know, complaints by VWS and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My earlier reference to the Registry was, of course, that portion of the Registry being VWS, which, of course, would have -- although it would -- acted the directions Trial Chamber, but the budgetary implications of all this is something that the Chamber could not -- could not not bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I use a double negative deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So far, Your Honours, VWS or nobody seems to have brought to the attention of the court that obviously bringing them up in time for the Defence to see them is costing a lot more because they are staying here longer, and therefore they get more daily subsistence allowance and the like. But, Your Honour, so leaving that aside for a moment, as I say, if Your Honours express the view that there is merit in what Mr. Zecevic says and that any drawbacks do not outweigh what he says, well, then, we'll continue to do it. So it really is as simple as that. But we thought it was important that Your Honours should be able to consider whether this is -- this is your being helped by this practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, counsel having raised the matter again, we would, of course, first of all, remind ourselves of what this Chamber would have said when this issue was last canvassed and also take on board the views of the Tribunal -- what the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is. And, if necessary, we would speak to this matter again. But I propose to leave it there for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the reason Mr. Zecevic wanted it raised today is the witness who is going do appear next week, if he is to be interviewed by the Defence as they request, and he accedes to here, then he will have to brought up at least a day earlier than he would otherwise be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have been more clear when I said for the time being. I didn't mean I would just leave the matter unresolved. But bearing in mind that the witness who was scheduled to testify today will be with us for the duration of the week, it is something that we will look at over the next day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm thankful to Your Honours for that. Now the second preliminary matter, I think it's going to be much shorter, and I think we have the agreement with the Office -- with our friend from the Prosecution side. Namely, here is the problem: We received the 92 ter package list for the coming witness, and I note that in this 92 ter package list, his statement given here in The Hague on the 25th of March 2010, after the proofing session, if Your Honours remember, he gave a statement where he changed his -- his position on certain -- three questions, which -- which are part of his 92 ter package. Now, if -- if I correctly understand, the practice of the Trial Chamber is all that proofing notes are disclosed to the -- to the Chamber, to the Bench. Now, this is his statement, he gave this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. It's a signed statement. It clearly contradicts some part of his testimony under 92 ter -- which is contained in the 92 ter package, and therefore I -- I requested from -- from my friends from the Prosecution the explanation why this particular statement is not part of the 92 ter package, because I think - and I hope you will agree with me - that this is the only logical way how we can proceed. If we want to have him as 92 ter witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I call on Ms. Korner, Mr. Zecevic, you, of course, have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which you understand to contradict in part a portion of the 92 ter package. And you were able to make such use of it in cross-examination as you choose. But you go further than that. You're saying that this has to be part of the -- because it modifies the -- yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no objection. I don't think it occurred to us because we were just using the same 92 ter package from before, and indeed it is absolutely clear that when I go through the -- the - I was going to say the song and dance routine - the routine of asking about the 92 ter transcript, I'm going have deal with the fact that he now says this is wrong. And I think Your Honours are going to have to see the actual parts. So clearly I think it should go in, and we just didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For my own edification, Ms. Korner, do I understand your position, and inferentially I gather that to be Mr. Zecevic's position, that the architecture of 92 ter includes, as in this case, where a witness makes a subsequent statement modifying in part or in whole what is in the 92 ter package, that that statement becomes part of the package?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now are we ready to have the usher escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And could you tell us your date of birth, your profession, and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 1st of May, 1954. I'm a Serb by ethnicity. And I have a university degree in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- you would have testified previously before this Tribunal, and, therefore, I need only remind you of the procedure which - and, again, you being a lawyer by profession - would not be unfamiliar with the practice of courts generally, that the side calling you would begin, in this case the Prosecution. The Defence would have a right to cross-examine, and then the Bench may have questions before you are released as a witness. Having testified previously before this Tribunal, you are called under an expedited Rule, which means that the Prosecution would be permitted to rely substantially on your previous testimony and would bring such of that previous testimony, as is relevant to the present trial, home to these proceedings by the questions it has of you, and to that extent, they have requested and been granted by the Chamber six hours to cross-examine you -- sorry, to lead you in-chief. The Defence cumulatively have -- have been allowed ten hours in cross-examination, and under the present schedule we -- we expect -- sorry. Ten plus two hours. And under the present schedule, we expect that you would be on the stand as a witness for most of this week. The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I address you just with a few words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just so you are aware, the matter has been raised as Their Honours said with the Registry here, and they are making inquiries as to why the matters that you described to the Judges have happened. So, for the moment, that's all we can tell you. Mr. Mandic, I want to start, please, by dealing with your -- how you came to be at this Court or you come to be at this Court again. I think it's right that matters began when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor with your rights given to you as a suspect, first of all, in May 2003; then in March 2004; and then in October 2004. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then testified in the case against Momcilo Krajisnik, between November of 2004, completing your testimony in December. In fact, a total of ten days in all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm going to come back to some of the charges that you've asked to make, or that you have made to your testimony in a moment. You came back, as the Court knows, to The Hague in March of this year, and then, for various reasons, you left after some five days here. During that period, were you seen by Defence counsel for Mico Stanisic, Mr. Zecevic, together with Mr. Cvijetic, and I think also Mr. Krgovic at some stage. And that was for a day, on Sunday, the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Only once. And that was with your consent or the consent of someone from the Prosecution, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not a criticism. I'm just setting the background. But is that right, you saw them on Sunday, the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you saw Mr. Zecevic again for some 30 minute this morning, before you had a short interview with us. All right. Did you -- before you left, on the last occasion on Thursday, the 25th of March, did you make a statement about some changes that you wanted to make to your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to run through a sort of outline of the things you testified before about. And this is not an exhaustive list by any means. But you testified obviously about your background and the positions you'd held. You testified about the establishment of the Serbian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the national security council; the leadership of the SDS; your knowledge, obviously, of Mico Stanisic; the division of the MUP; the 11th of February meeting that was held in Banja Luka; the dispatch that you sent on the 31st of March; arming; the attack on Vrace school; dismissals; the autonomous regions; the camps, or detention facilities; what sort of communication there was and what notice you were receiving of what was happening; the council of ministers; Crisis Staffs; obviously, the Ministry of Justice; prisons; courts; prisoner exchanges; and paramilitary. So you covered a very large range of topics. Is that right, Mr. Mandic, when you testified in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: With only one exception, Madam Prosecutor. I never said there had been an attack by the Serbian police on Vrace. It was not an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me -- I agree. I will change the word it was the occupation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The rest of the topics I did cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I can explain when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you now about the three matters that you wanted to make some changes to. And this is the statement that you made -- short statement, which you signed. The first thing that you wanted to alter was what you had said about the -- yes, we've got duplicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think perhaps we have got it in Sanction so that Your Honours can see it and Mr. Mandic can see it as well. And the first paragraph -- go to paragraph 1, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you can see there what you wanted to change, and I think we need to look, for a moment, at how this came about in your previous testimony. You were actually shown a document which is part of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, part of the 92 ter package, and it's 1402 on the 65 ter list, tab 28, if you've got it. So could we have up, please, 65 ter 1402.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was a -- you were being shown this document which is the central commission for the exchange of prisoners, and it was signed by a captain who said at the bottom of the paragraph: "According to rough estimates, about 10.000 Muslim civilians (of all ages) passed through this facility during the war, spending between several days and a few months in this facility." That was what the document said. And the question you were asked by Mr. Tieger at page 8741 was -- really, 8742. He said: "I simply wanted to know if based on your own experience you had any reason to doubt the accuracy of the figures in here or the accuracy of the assertion that from the commencement of the war civilians were detained in Butmir." And you said: "This document was signed by Dragan Bulajic who was president of the commission for exchange, and I have no reason to doubt that the contents of this document ..." And it was written towards the end of 1994. Now, so it wasn't exactly that you said it; it was what was contained in this document. And you've now said that you, to your knowledge among, those 10.000 people were locals who would hide there for safety and to get food, and it was located next to a chicken farm. And then also: "Since this prison was close to the airport where prisoner exchanges were being carried out, the people being exchanged would all pass through Butmir prison from all over the republic." All right. Is there anything that -- that you want to add to -- to that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I had forgotten that in my testimony in Krajisnik I explained these things in this way. Namely, that through the buildings of the farm that was close to the airport civilians who were fleeing combat zones were passing through, and there were also people who were coming there for food, because there were food shortages at the time. So it did not refer to people detained on those premises. In other cases, it was established exactly how many non-Serbs were detained in Butmir at precisely what time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I suppose the question is: This was -- all can you say in respect of this document is that was a document that was sent up and signed by this gentleman. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was two years after I left for Belgrade, and it was the President of the Central Commission for Exchanges of POWs, Ljubisa Bladosic [phoen] was at the time commissioner for refugees, and he requested food for those people from the government, the people who provisionally spent time on those premises, because the premises of that detention and correctional facility were in the immediate vicinity of the airport, of an area where exchanges between the warring parties took place. And before exchanges they had to spend a certain time in a -- in some lotion, and this was the most suitable facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave that then and go to the second correction you wanted to make, where you said: "I was told that in my prior testimony the transcript reads that I said that the police would detain people for 30 days." Now, is this something that you were told by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think I read it, or perhaps the Defence pointed it out. I can't remember. But it's obviously a mistake, because the police could not keep anyone in custody for 30 days. Only up to three days under the Law on Criminal Procedure. Only a judge, an investigating judge, could decide to prolong the remand. So it must be a mistake that I made in my language, or it's a typo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well I'll show you how this came about, you see. I'm not sure the Defence explained to you exactly how this came about. You were actually been shown -- and this is at page 8948 of the transcript, although there's a lot of interruption by Mr. Stewart who was defending, so it is a bit truncated. You were being shown a particular document, which was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm just going to ... In fact, 65 ter 176, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we can have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. In the 92 ter -- it is 44 in the 92 ter package. That's P427.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the document was first shown to you, just for the purposes of everybody's note if they want to check it, at 8943. It's day five of the testimony. And as I say, there's a lot of to-ing and fro-ing about the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then, can we go in the English, please, to -- this is a document called before -- a report on some aspects of the work done to date and tasks ahead, and it's dated -- it's Sarajevo the 17th of July. And if we look, please, in the English - one, two, three, four - fifth page and I hope in the B/C/S, because I don't have that with me, unfortunately. Sixth page, sorry. Yes. One more page. That's it. And it's the paragraph beginning with: "A view to resolving existing problems ..." And I can't even work this one out because it is in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the penultimate page in Cyrillic? Mr. Mandic, do you see a paragraph that begins: "With a view to resolving existing problems ..."?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And four or five lines down, it says this: "With a view to resolving existing problems ... joint meeting to reach an agreement on initiating proceedings for changing the duration of pre-trial detention, the Presidency should uphold the provision according to which detention can last up to 31 days." Now I hope that's what it says in Serbian as well. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says 21, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, okay, 21. Yeah, I think that was the decision in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Mandic, it says 21?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, what -- what was happening was that there was a discussion about this particular document, and -- and you give your answer on page 8948 of the transcript. But anyhow you're saying, are you, that at no stage did the length of time which the MUP could people -- could keep people in detention for change to longer than three days?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the final one, perhaps this does need a little more explanation from you, please. Your final change: "In my prior testimony and statement, I said that Mico Stanisic instructed me to send the dispatch on the 31st of March, 1992, advising of the split in the MUP. I wrote the dispatch. It was logical for the minister of the interior to instruct me to do this, but did he not. I was in charge of the Serbs in the MUP at the time and did not write this dispatch on anyone's behalf. I received information from Velibor Ostojic that the law had a had been passed in accordance with the Cutileiro Plan, and I wrote this on my own initiative in accordance with my own conscience and professionalism and in cooperation with the professionals in my cabinet." Now, Mr. Mandic, before you just expand on that, I think we had better just look at what you did say about this during your testimony. The first part is at 8677, which is on day 2. You had been shown the dispatch, and you were asked this -- there was a legal argument again. Mr. Tieger said: "Mr. Mandic, at the time you sent the document, did you realise or believe that the dissemination of this document would commence the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina? And you said: "No, I only acted in accordance to the decisions of the Serbian people, on 27th of March, 1992, passed such a decision and also the Law on Interior. Since I was a high-ranking administration official - or, actually, in terms of rank the top official in the joint MUP - I was instructed by the newly appointed minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, to send this kind of telegram, and that's what I did." And then you were asked about this again, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, who you probably remember, at page 9314. Mr. Stewart said to you: "And you have given evidence that, as far as you were concerned, this was in accordance with decisions which had already been taken on behalf of the Serbian people. But Mr. Krajisnik had no -- himself had no individual part in the preparation and dissemination of this particular document, did he? And you answered: "You're right. At that moment, Mr. Krajisnik was in Lisbon together with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and I believe Mate Boban, where they signed the so-called Cutileiro Plan. This plan verified" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Ms. Korner, I'm -- I'm reading the page 9314, and I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bottom answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "This plan verified the creation of armies and police forces based on ethnicity and Mr. Stanisic informed me about this. He said that in keeping with the decisions of the Assembly and the enactments stated in the dispatch, I was supposed to circulate this across all the territory to all police stations and all autonomous regions." And you had said much the same in your interview, which is not -- your previous interview, which not part of the package. Now, Mr. Mandic, when did you decide that you had made an error in saying it was Mico Stanisic who instructed you to send the dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I spoke about this in the Krajisnik case, and following logic, I should have consulted the newly appointed minister of police. However, after thinking it through, and looking at the documents, I recalled that I had been informed by this by Velibor Ostojic, the then information minister. Then, on the 23rd of March, in the Official Gazette of the Serbian People the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska was published, and he told me that it came into force eight days after the publication. Following the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian people, it was my duty to notify everyone from the very top to the last police station in whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the forming of the Serbian MUP. Stanisic had nothing to do with that, nor did he have anything to do with that. And I swear to this with my honour. I made a mistake. I didn't pay much attention whether it was Stanisic or Velibor Ostojic, but now today I want to say the truth, and this is the truth. And I would take this opportunity to apologise both to Mr. Stanisic and to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it after or before you spoke to the Defence on the Sunday that you came to the conclusion that you'd made this mistake?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The Defence raised some objections with me, and that prompted me to think about the chain of events. You know, in the Krajisnik case, I think that I gave evidence for ten or 12 days in a row. I was overtired, exhausted, and I was focussed on other things, rather than in mentioning in a context either the minister of information or the minister of police. But the fact is that this dispatch was sent from my office, that I drafted it with my associate, the fact that the Law on Internal Affairs came into effect, and the fact is that it was pursuant to the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People. So, Madam Prosecutor, at this juncture, this was sanctioned by Dayton Accords, and currently this is the hierarchy existing in the MUP of the Republika Srpska, and this was also sanctioned at the moment by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nothing has changed. Of course, you haven't received the supplement to my telegram, providing details about education, finances, health care, et cetera, which were agreed at the staff meeting in the ministry that all these costs relating to health, education, et cetera, be pooled until a political decision was made about how to construct the police forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just have two further questions on this, Mr. Mandic. The first is: Where was Mico Stanisic at the time that you sent the telegram? Dispatch, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think that he was on holiday, that he wasn't in any of the police institutions at the time. He had been a minor official in the city of Sarajevo. He was given a new post of an advisor to the minister, and he went on holiday. Therefore, he was not in touch with me whatsoever. It was only the minister of information and people who worked in the joint MUP. The Croats and the Muslims were the ones who kept communication with me, including the Serbs. I think that was the situation. Yes, he was on vacation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, just two things. By 31st of March 1992, he had been appointed the minister of the interior, hadn't he? His appointment had come on the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know when he was appointed. I was informed that he had become the minister of police by necessity. Vito Zepinic was the minister of police, and it was published in the Official Gazette. Since Mr. Zepinic was prone to corruption, the president of the council and the future prime minister, probably in agreement with the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, that Mico Stanisic should become the minister. He was an ad hoc minister. Vitomir Zepinic was the Serbian -- proper Serbian minister of the police, and that was published in the Official Gazette. But, having found that he was a corrupt person, that he had been given by the party of democratic action some offices and something like that, it was decided, I don't know on what basis, that Mico Stanisic should be appointed. He was a member of the Ministerial council without any portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic had been the -- the second in command, had he not, deputy, to Mr. Delimustafic in the old undivided MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that's correct, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when it was decided at the Assembly of the 27th of March to split the MUP, enact the Serbian law on the MUP, weren't you aware -- are you telling us you weren't aware that Mr. Stanisic was appointed as minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: He was nominated as a candidate for the minister because Vito Zepinic was found by the service to be corrupt, that he had taken bribes from the Party of Democratic Action, or, rather, the political leadership of the Muslim people. That was the only reason. Because Vitomir Zepinic was appointed, number one, in the police by the ministerial council, and that was published in the Official Gazette of January 1992 [realtime transcript read in error "1993"]. And I believe that Mico Stanisic was a member of the council without any portfolio. I think so; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we are getting slightly muddled, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point to take the break? Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have one intervention in the transcript, line 3, I believe the witness said January 1992, and I think it might be important further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he is talking about the ministerial council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ministerial council, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, it's December 1991, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but it was published in Official Gazette of Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina in January 1992. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I said, we're going slightly at cross-purposes here, I think. But, Your Honours, yes, it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered, may I just, for the purposes of transcript, announce that Kenneth Janesk has joined -- our associate has joined the Stanisic Defence. In another matter, Your Honour, I briefly discussed with my learned friends from the Prosecution, I believe -- your decision of today on page 16, line 9, until 18, line 1, is in a private session, that was the part when the witness was -- was giving his explanation or his complaint to the Trial Chamber. I don't think -- I don't think that this part should be -- should be private, and I will request, kindly, the Trial Chamber to reconsider that, and make that part of the transcript public. There is no objection, as I understand, from the -- from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's right, there's no objection. I mean, Your Honours decided to go into private session. Nobody requested it. But we don't have any strong views, can we put it that way. We're neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We thought when we moved into the private session earlier on this afternoon that the witness was going to address issues that would relate to a foreign government. And for that reason we thought it wise to go into private session, but we haven't had a chance to review what was actually said during this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he did mention a foreign government, there's no doubt about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We suggest we review the transcript and then get back with a decision on your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I'm grateful to Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, all right. That's all that I want to ask you about the corrections that you made. We can sort out the slight confusion over Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Stanisic and the Council of Ministers a little later. As far as the remainder of the transcript of your previous testimony is concerned, have you now reviewed either by listening or by reading what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I have read it, and I fully comply with the statement that I gave in the Krajisnik says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So have you no other changes to make?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the -- if you were asked the same questions again, which you're not going to be, I can assure you, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: They would be the same. But if I have forgotten something, I would appreciate if you would remind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in those circumstances can I ask that the 92 ter package be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1318.1 through .36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm afraid, as you appreciate, Mr. Mandic, we're going to have to take you through some other --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I didn't object, but if Your Honours remember at the very beginning, I asked that his statement be part of the 92 ter package. I don't know if it -- if it has been done. Oh, I see that from the Registry that it has been done. Thank you very much, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, the only one that's been admitted -- his previous interviews were not part of the package. That's the interviews he had with the Office of the Prosecutor. The only thing that has been added is the statement he made on the 25th of March, corrections to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I just need to deal with few matters that you personally brought up. One is your acquittal at the State Court. So if we could just deal with that so that the Trial Chamber has the full picture. I think that you were arrested on 17th of August of 2005 in Montenegro. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I was abducted from my flat, and within a space of two hours, I was transferred to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina without any documents whatsoever, without any right to extraditionary [as interpreted] detention, and at the time I was a citizen of the Montenegro. So that was classic case of abduction by unknown individuals who abducted me in a brutal way and took me across the border between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, in a helicopter owned by international community, I was transferred to a prison in Sarajevo. This was something totally different from the notion of arrest. I was abducted. It was an abduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My fault. I perhaps used the wrong word. In any event, as you say, you were transferred, by means that you described, to Sarajevo. You were held in custody. An indictment was filed on the 20th of January, 2006. But not in relation to war crimes; it was in relation to your job as a -- as the director of the Privredna Banka Srpska Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. Among other things I was indicted at the time for aiding The Hague fugitive, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And I also accused of extending loans to certain Serbian companies which then used this money to provide a hideout for Mr. Karadzic and for him to evade justice. I am an owner of that bank, although I was indicted for allegedly hiding Mr. Karadzic, I was falsely accused of extending loans from my own bank to the Serbian companies that were aiding and abetting Mr. Karadzic. Unfortunately, that is how the judiciary worked at the time. Although I served part of my sentence, I am now free. I don't feel that that was justice done. There was no precedent in any legal system, and that was the reason for my dissatisfaction, because they wanted to put me in prison as the main integrator of providing shelter to Mr. Karadzic, and I do not acknowledge that judgement and that conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I assume that is because the witness talks pretty fast that the interpreters are not able to cope with the pace. So if Ms. Korner can instruct him to speak a bit slower so -- so the transcript will reflect exactly what he said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, the -- what you -- you're speaking in B/C/S and what -- your testimony has to be interrupted for the purposes of the transcript, and to aid in the accuracy of that, if you would be so kind as to slow down the pace a bit that you're speaking, that would be of assistance to us all. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You heard, Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right. I was going to come on to that because, as you say rightly, in fact you were also charged in relation to forgery of an official document as -- in connection with a copy called Autorad Trebinje, and as you say, roughly speaking, and we have the indictment here, if the Court need to see it, with helping Karadzic. Now, on the 27th of October 2006, they found you guilty, the court, of abuse of your official authority and forgery of the document. You were not found guilty of anything to do with Karadzic. And at that stage they sentenced you to nine years imprisonment, but that was reduced on appeal to five years. Then in the middle of that trial, you were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity. The charges related there to the takeover of Vrace school - not going call it an attack - on the 6th of April, unlawful confinement and ill-treatment of civilians and conditions, and in respect of the treatment of people in the Butmir prison, Planja's House in Vogosca, and in Foca. And as you told the Court, you were acquitted of those war crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: If you permit me a couple of explanations. I was a suspect in this court. And on a couple of occasions, the investigators from this Tribunal talked to me about this. In the meantime my case had been filed by this Prosecution office when Carla Del Ponte was the Prosecutor. It was filed with [as interpreted] any markings whatsoever, which means that there were no elements for criminal prosecution. There was no A, B, or C. In the meantime the rule of the Rome road [as interpreted] ceased to exist, which provided for the Prosecution in Bosnia and Herzegovina to ask this Prosecution, regarding anyone, to re-open the case or to issue an indictment. This took place on the 31st of December, 2004, when this provision ceased to be in force. Since I was there at the time, an indictment was immediately issued against me. I was transferred from the cantonal Prosecutor's office to the Prosecution office of BH. And without a single shred of evidence, an indictment was issued. All the elements that the Prosecutor in Sarajevo had was provided from here, and they were marked as a source, the OTP of the The Hague Tribunal. Of course, the intention was just to establish and just to bind me to help locate Dr. Karadzic, because, in the meantime, an associate of The Hague Tribunal appeared in court and talked to me about this subject. They tried to persuade me to say where Karadzic was, what his health condition was, et cetera, and that that would result in the acquittal of my -- of the both indictment -- the indictments. And I was eventually released, and I'm deeply convinced that this proceedings should never have taken place at all, because I was the only head of an administrative organ that had been the subject of a criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That -- well, Mr. Mandic, yeah, you've now explained what happened from your point of view. Can I, just very briefly for the purpose of the Court, cover the positions you held for the period we are interested in. I think you attended the police school in Sarajevo. Was that together with Mico Stanisic, or one of people there was Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were in the same class in the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think you then worked for the SUP in Sarajevo, then attended university where you read law. And did you subsequently receive an MA in 1989, the subject of your dissertation being the role of the witness in criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, the role of the witness in the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sure everybody in the court sees in the irony of that, Mr. Mandic. Then were you a judge in the basic court until 1991, did you become the assistant minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I was elected the judge of the cantonal court, which was then called the higher court. But instead of that, I became assistant minister for the interior at the proposal and suggestion of Dr. Vitomir Zepinic. But, as my side activity, I was involved in sports for many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was just going to come on to that. I think you were in fact the Yugoslav champion for judo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: And I also won the European medal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then in April 1992, were you appointed deputy minister of the interior, and then on 19th of May, the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I was never appointed Deputy Minister of the interior, nor did this place exist or this position exist in the job classification of the newly formed Serbian MUP. But the then-minister Mico Stanisic agreed with me that I would act as his stand-in and to assist him in the work of the MUP. That was an arrangement between the Serbian police minister and me as an assistant, who had, at the moment, lost his job in the joint MUP, because on 8th of April, I was dismissed at the session of the joint government of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was chaired by Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just an intervention in the transcript, page 37, line 18, I believe the witness said that after he was judge of the cantonal court, he was supposed to go to the higher court, but instead of that he went to -- he became assistant minister for the interior. Just for the clarity of the transcript. Maybe you can check it out with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, wrong, Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer from the beginning, slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The interpreters would wish you to repeat your answer from the beginning slowly, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About your judicial appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of 1990, I was a judge with the lower court in Sarajevo. At the time I was elected to the position in the higher court in Sarajevo. In the meantime this higher court changed name, and it was called then and now the cantonal court. It's a higher-instance. The court takes more serious crimes than the lower court. And instead of taking up that position, I -- I became assistant minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I think that is now clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you remain as minister of justice from the 19th of May, 1992, as part of the government headed by Mr. Djeric until that government fell in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then before we move to some of the documents I'd like to ask you about, can I ask you just to look at some maps. And I just wanted to -- for the Trial Chamber to see an idea of what Pale and Jahorina were like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can we have up 10346. No, 10346, please. Page 3, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is, as I think everyone can see, taken from Google maps, but it seems to be the simplest way of portraying this. Can we see that Sarajevo, in the dip there -- and it's all marked. Pale, you have to go up over the mountains. And then Jahorina, even higher up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we look, please, at 10346, page 2. Which can only be said to be slightly better than the skiing map, but anyhow ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you put out to us, please -- we can see there the Bistrica hotel. Where is that? You can draw on to the screen, if you can just mark that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And the Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put 1 in the first circle you made, which is the Bistrica; and 2 for the Jahorina. Thanks. Who or what was based in the Bistrica hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The government led by Professor Djeric was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that where your office was, as minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the Jahorina hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think the refugees were put up in Hotel Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, on the series of maps, could we look at 10346, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the first map showing the various locations of Pale, Sarajevo, and Jahorina admitted and marked. I can't have them all three marked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the 10346 is on your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely spot on. But are you telling me that there is an objection to a map from Google maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not objecting to the -- to the document itself. I'm objecting as regarding the principle that we have, how to -- how to admit the documents which are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a sense of reality about this. We understand if it's a document where -- we've had our collections and it's a -- but this is just a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is this of any material assistance to the Chamber to have this map? I mean, regardless of the fact of whether or not it was on the 65 ter list, are we learning something new here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you've got any. As far as I remember, there aren't any maps of Pale, and Your Honours are going to hear quite a lot of evidence and have heard quite a lot evidence about the relative where Jahorina is in relation to Pale and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Don't we have geographical maps that show exactly where these cities are?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't think so. No you've just got -- yes, Your Honours -- It -- all you have got is this. And if that gives you any assistance at all, I should be very surprised. I'm afraid we did rather more research now than we did before the pre-trial brief. It's page -- map 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the -- it seems to me that the -- inasmuch as Google has become ubiquitous, that this is -- falls into the category of things of which judicial notice can be taken, so it's merely a matter of the Prosecution moving something out of the public domain and marking it for our purposes, so I see no reason not to give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In that case, could the first one, which was the Google map, Sarajevo, pale, and whatever, be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could I have the plain unmarked map of the Bistrik hotel and Jahorina, the one that was on the screen but has disappeared suddenly, as the next exhibit; plus, as a separate exhibit, the one that he marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I gather that ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, can we have the three pages, one as one exhibit; and the one that Mr. Mandic marked as the second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Unmarked map, three pages of it, will become Exhibit P1319. And the marked map with markings will become Exhibit P1320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally can I ask you to look at the street plan of Pale. Oh, page 1. I'm not going to ask you because one needs to zoom in, and I don't want to waste time on that. In the Karadzic residence we can see there, the photograph at the bottom left, who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Is this the residence or a residential house? This is an official residence, I think, where the office of Mr. Karadzic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did anybody else have offices there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: If that's the building I mean, then Dr. Karadzic was on the ground floor, and Momcilo Krajisnik was on the upper floor. So the Assembly was on the upper floor and the office of the president of the Republika Srpska on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. On the right-hand side, we can see Panorama and the Mali Dom. Can you just indicate again, can you just mark it, please, where was the Hotel Panorama?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is the official residence, Mali Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you put down 1, please, where the Mali Dom; and 2 for the Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I'm going trouble with you about maps and plans. Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, and could that be tendered, please, separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I now need to ask you about some other documents that you had a chance to have a look at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we start, please, with -- yes, 2401.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this doesn't seem to have a date on it, but I think you were able, when you looked at it, to tell us what date this was, or what date you thought it was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's somewhere between mid-April to end April 1992. Between the 10th and 19th, perhaps, 20th, of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you are able to say that how?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's because I was standing in for the minister between the 10th and the 20th of April, when I was informed I would take over the Ministry of Justice, because the minister, Ranko Nikolic, who had been elected minister of justice at the Ministerial Council failed to show up at his post.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who did you say the minister? Which minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Ranko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And is that your signature on -- by the side of the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I cannot identify it. You mean the one below? At the bottom? It's someone called Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the one, I'm sorry, by the side where you are signing for you salary. Are you able to identify that number 9? It's very squashed; I agree.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't. It probably is. But I cannot identify it because there's a -- a signature superimposed on mine. But there's no reason to doubt that it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's from the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could we -- I just want to check something on the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the next thing I want to ask you -- no, that's been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry. I prepared this before I realised that some of these documents have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, can I ask you to look, please, at the transcript of a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, which is 33 -- sorry. Yes, it's 3397.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because I don't believe, Your Honours, we've yet had -- or those haven't been admitted, the intercepts given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which reminds me, the Chamber would have filed a decision today clarifying its earlier decision in terms of these exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now you listened to this one this morning. We didn't give you the transcript, Mr. Mandic, but I think you were able to identify the voices of -- recognise the voices of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. But it's some of the things that were said about you that I want to ask you about. Mr. Krajisnik is having a conversation, to begin with, to do with an attack on the Serbian village of Kravica. And then if we can go on to the second page in both, Mr. Krajisnik says: "I told Vito to make sure he goes there to put in an appearance before the people. There are people. You know, they've become agitated. They want an army." Do you know from the context who the Vito was that Mr. Krajisnik was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Most probably Vitomir Zepinic, Deputy Minister of the joint MUP. We called him Vito.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then Mr. Karadzic says: "We'll make our point." And he says: "Can you see where this leads? Do your realise you will disappear?" And then he goes on say: "Many of us will also disappear, but you will be annihilated." And then Mr. Krajisnik says: "No we should say we'd all disappear." Now leaving all that aside, can we go down to where it says Mr. Krajisnik says this: "Not cunning, you know what happened last night. You weren't there. You'd gone out when Momcilo Mandic said, Please you're not doing things properly. He said, no one's doing things properly. And before that I'd told him, you know, that none of them were doing things properly." And then there's a bit more to it. And then Mr. Krajisnik says again: "I didn't want to undermine their authority, you know, and they said you're right. And then Mandic started going on about how Draskovic isn't doing anything, he's resolving staff problems and not working on this." Now Mr. Mandic, looking at this, can you us what it was that, if you can remember - and this conversation is the 4th of September of 1991 - what Mr. Krajisnik is saying you were objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know what it was about. I really can't. It was September 1991. There's a reference to Draskovic, who, at the time, was deputy chief of the police, deputy to Avdo Hebib. No, I don't know. I don't know which line of work this refers to, which service. Is it personnel or crime police, regular uniformed police? I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recall any time around this period, which is we know leading up to what happened in October when the Assembly effectively split, where you were saying to Mr. Krajisnik, Look, you're not doing any of this properly? Do you remember any occasions saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think can I take this much further. All right. Can we move then, please, next, to -- let me just check ... yeah, this is another intercept, this time between Mr. -- sorry, the number is 1049.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the last page in English and in B/C/S. And this is Simovic saying: "I asked for Momo Mandic to go" -- this is to Capljina. "If somebody from the SDS had to go, I was in favour of either Mico Stanisic or Mandic; however, we could not get a hold of either of them. And I said that if they were not there, you would not go either." Two things, please. Were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Is there any -- I was going to say is there any point in me asking. Can you recall anything about what this might refer to on the 28th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: There was something going on in Capljina. I believe Simovic confused Serbian personnel and the SDS. He probably meant the Serbian personnel elected by the party in power, the Serbian Democratic Party, people from the SDS and senior executives elected by the party in power, and Simovic was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you very much. I'd like you to look, please, next, at a document you sent to Mr. Karadzic on 16th of October, which is document 65 ter 2703. Now, this is a report, and is that your signature on it, Mr. Mandic, or is it somebody signing on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, that's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. Nope. Let me see inside the report. But this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but is it on your behalf apparently? Does it say "za"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now this is apparently, we can see, on the 3rd of September 1991, 17 workers sent a memorandum to the Ministry of the Interior alleging that a former director of the company, Mico Stanisic, had ruined the enterprise which his - I think it must be his unscrupulousness, but apart from that - and incompetence. Then there was petition, and so on. Do you remember this now, because in fact --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic was never the director of the trading company in Rajlovac. He was a legal advisor, an administrative officer, while the director of that trading company was a Muslim. I can't remember the name. He is now a lawyer in Sarajevo. I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- sorry, Mr. Mandic. The ins and outs of what was happening are not the purpose --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you. Are you saying this is not a report that you did?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I did not. I'm seeing this for the first time in my life. Or I'm drawing a complete blank after 17 years. Because I know when Mico left the police he was a legal advisor in this company which held the commodity reserves of the city of Sarajevo. He was assistant or a deputy perhaps, but never the director. I cannot recall the name of the real director, but it will come to me. He was, until the beginning of the war, the director of a commodity reserves. He was Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can I say -- Mr. Mandic, just let me finish for a moment. First of all, as I say, the ins and outs of this allegation are not relevant to this trial. But what is relevant and why I'm asking you this is why this report was sent to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't see why this would be addressed to Karadzic. It's a report on crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's -- it doesn't make sense. I would never do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Karadzic was not in power at the time. He was just a party boss at the time. If this letter was to be sent anywhere, the right address would the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the front page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at -- at the stamp. What is that the sampling of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't see it. It's some secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. What about -- does that -- is that somebody who says that he is signing on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I find this rather illegible. Something is written at the bottom. Does it say: "Za"? No, this is not my signature. That is certain. Look at the all the documents. I never signed it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you did. But somebody, whoever signed it, says "za"? Does that not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now do you know anything about any allegations that were made against Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I can only give you my personal opinion. It needn't be correct. Somebody wanted to prevent Stanisic from coming to the police so he was set up and accused of committing a crime. I would say that was something typical in Bosnia or amongst Serbs. To send such a report to the leader of the party just to -- to show how the structure of power in Bosnia-Herzegovina existed, I don't see anything in the then Law on the Criminal Procedure that this kind of report would be sent to the leader of the party about any fraudulent activities in any company.
