And I think that already at the time Mico Stanisic was with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, I just -- I'm just not sure where you see "for" on this document. I see there assistant minister of the interior, and it says in Serbian [B/C/S] spoken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the last bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says, MR. Momcilo Mandic. I believe MR stands for magistrate. Magistrate of law. That's academic -- I think that's -- maybe you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you have heard what Mr. Zecevic has said. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I mean, I agree, I had an MA at the time, but, believe me, this is not my signature. This is not my letter. I would never have sent a letter to the party, to a political party. It doesn't make sense. And all my letters were drafted by my assistants -- assistants in charge of general crime, economic crime, et cetera. I had different lines of works, and I had people who were responsible for those lines of work. You can see who signed the document itself. This is just a covering letter. Let's see who signed the main document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know somebody called Momcilo Janjetovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, he was chased out of the police when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an inspector. I don't know. He ended up. And he was never employed in the police administration. He used to work in some of the lower organs of the police administrations, whether in the SUP of the city or the security centre. But this person never worked in my administration that was in the headquarters of the ministry, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but if there was a report -- and I don't want to spend too much time on this. But if there was report on an allegation of crime involving a senior person in a company or a senior police officer, would such a report have to be sent to you as the assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: If it went out lawfully from my administration, I would be the one to sign it. But this person never worked in my administration. You can check that. Ask for the list of personnel of the criminal investigation department in the police headquarters in 1991. There was no Momcilo Janjetovic working in my administration. He was a member of the police, though. But he worked in some of the lower ranking centres, either in the centre of Sarajevo or Sarajevo SUP, or even a police station in Sarajevo. But never in the administration where I was the chief and where I was directly overseeing the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Anyhow, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes he was. At least I think so. Momcilo is a Serbian first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Can you think of any reason why such a report should be sent to Mr. Karadzic? Any lawfully reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: There could be no lawful reason. The only objective could be to inform one of the leaders of the ruling parties about a person who was supposed to join the police that he was not an honest man. These were just framing up people. There was no criminal report, and Mico Stanisic was never processed with regard to the commodity reserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, as I said to you, I have no interest in whether this was a genuine or false allegation. My only query is why this should have gone to Karadzic. Did Mr. Karadzic, from your knowledge of him, take an interest in Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... in other words, was Mr. Karadzic particularly interested in Mr. Stanisic in -- in respect of having him in the police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of the personnel policy, as far as the Serbs are concerned. I had no suggestions from Mr. Karadzic. I only had suggestions from the local people in powers, and both my colleagues, Muslims and Croats had problems with that. As far as Mr. Karadzic is concerned, he never called me and asked me to appoint anyone. Anyway, there was a totally different procedure of appointing lower-ranking officers in the police. The leadership of any party, including the ruling party, decided only about the top positions in the ministry. The first five positions. Everything else was nominated and decided by regional political leaderships of the three ruling parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. We in the MUP headquarters would decide who would be appointed to each position. I was never in my life asked about Mico Stanisic by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't think I can do much with it at this stage except to ask to be marked for identification, even though he has recognised the signature, or the -- sorry, one last question before we leave the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does the stamp look, to you, like the stamp that you used?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam Prosecutor. I can't recognise the signature, but the name of Momcilo Janjetovic I know. I know who this is. I don't know whether this is his signature or not. I know that this man existed, and I know that he was employed in lower-ranking bodies of the police, but I have never seen his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe there is enough grounds even for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I finish? I haven't finished. I have not finished on the document. I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry I thought you offered it for MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, one last question. Can I go back to the stamp, please. On the front page. First page in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you have another look at it and tell us whether that is in fact the stamp of your ministry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: You see that it says the regional secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. So is that your stamp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. Of course it's not. My headquarters were at the republican level, not regional. And it says here the centre -- this secretariat -- well, this seal was not used by the Ministry of the Interior. This was the stamp of a lower-ranking organisational unit. It says here "centre," whereas, where I worked, it was called "administration." And I had no secretariat whatsoever. You can see here on the top, it says, "secretariat," Madam Prosecutor. I didn't have any secretariats. I only had an administration within the ministry. So this is not the stamp that was used at the ministry headquarters. This is a security centre, probably the Sarajevo security centre. It's a totally different local organisational unit. It is nothing to do with the ministry. You see, it says here, "secretariat," and then below, you see the word "centre." I really don't know. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mandic, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't have -- well, I do have a strong view. I think it should be marked for identification. I certainly can't have it admitted at this stage as an exhibit; I accept that. But we have asked a lot of questions about, and he knows, at the very at least - just a moment Mr. Zecevic - the guy who compiled report. Now can you object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm really sorry, I thought you finished already. Your Honours, my objection is that this document be MFI'd at all. This document allegedly is signed by this witness. The witness confirms that it's not his signature. He never saw the document. The person who -- who allegedly wrote the report was never employed in his administration, and he -- he claims that the -- that the -- that the stamp is -- is not of his administration. Therefore, I don't see -- I don't see any -- any reason whatsoever that we -- that we can -- that this document reaches the threshold to be MFI'd, that's all, at this point at least. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with Mr. Zecevic. This -- the Prosecution may have to return to this document through another witness. But as far as this witness goes, it doesn't, as Mr. Zecevic has said, even reach a threshold to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, then, can I just make sure it's on the record, so if we do decide to go back to it -- it's a document dated 16th October, 1991, and it has the ERN number SA023297. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, then, Mr. Mandic, can we ask you, please, to have a look at - yes - some Assembly minutes. Now, can I ask you, first of all, did you attend the Assemblies of the Serbian People during the course of 1992 as a minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Very frequently. Quite often. I may not have attended all of the Assembly sessions, but I was there very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, can I ask you, please, to have a look at part of the record of the Assembly of the 25th of February, 1992, which is 914 -- sorry, P427.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. It's 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, first of all, about something that Savo Knezovic said. You knew Savo Knezovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that man. Probably he was a deputy. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The ex-Orthodox priest. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a very practicing religious person at that time, and I didn't know any priests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, well, can we look, please -- well, no, he wasn't a priest at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 48 in the English; and in the B/C/S, it's got 61 at the top. And it is the second paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezovic was saying that: "Until very recently we were saying that the Yugoslav Army which we consider almost a Serbian army, that that army would protect Serbian interests in all parts of Yugoslavia." Now was that something that you thought as well, that the Yugoslav Army was -- was a Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I didn't think that the Yugoslav Army was a Serb army. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did -- did anyone -- well, here Mr. Knezovic saying: "What about others, Mr. Karadzic, for example?"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know what -- what either Knezovic or Karadzic thought. The Yugoslav Army was composed of members of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know how Mr. Knezovic came to be saying that, because he says: "Until very recently, we were saying that the Yugoslav Army, which we consider almost a Serbian army."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know who this person Knezovic is. If he wasn't a deputy, what was he? I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know who Savo Knezovic is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move on to somebody who you did know. Mr. Dukic. You did know Mr. Dukic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: You mean General Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Rajko Dukic. If we can go to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's Rajko Dukic. Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... can we move, then, please, to the next page in English; and in B/C/S, it's on page 63. It's two pages on. All right. Mr. Dukic decides to give some figures. In 1971, 37 of the population was Serb; 39 per cent Muslim. In 1981, Serbs made up 32 per cent, and Muslim 39. And you know the data, et cetera, for 1991. Which means by the time the next census, Muslims will account for 51 per cent and Serbs for 27. This means that in a state like that, where it was possible to have this kind of demographic explosion, that we would be put in a position where others would have an absolute majority and where they could make decisions about all issues in their favour without difficulty. Now, Mr. Mandic, was that something that was discussed on a number of occasions that it would appear that the Muslims were demographically exploding, as, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the year that these minutes were taken? Was that an Assembly session, or was it a meeting of the political leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It was the Assembly on 25th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It was only in February that I met Rajko Dukic. I saw him for the first time then. He was a mining engineer. I don't know where he came -- where he got this information. Everybody was playing with statistics. This man was in charge of the bauxite mine in Milici, and in early 1991 he was at the head of the personnel commission who interviewed me and who agreed with my appointment to the position of the assistant minister. How come that he is talking about demographic issues, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, now, Mr. Mandic, concentrate on the question. I wasn't asking about Mr. Dukic, although I will come back to that in a moment. I was asking whether at the Assembly sessions you were attending and other meetings, the so-called population explosion of the Muslims was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now next, let's return to Mr. Dukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when you reach a convenient point, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm more or less --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He in fact, did he not, and certainly at the time of the barricades incident in March, was head of the SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And he was the president of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party which is number two in the Serbian party after Dr. Radovan Karadzic. As far as the Serbian Democratic Party was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, well, I've just got -- Your Honours, if can I just finish this document, and that's the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one other quote. Could we move to Mr. Kupresanin. Did you know him, Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Not person. I knew that he was from the Krajina, that he was some official from the SAO Krajina. I personally didn't know him, but I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, in English at page 59, and in B/C/S, at 74. Mr. Kupresanin says -- it's the -- yeah, fourth paragraph in B/C/S. And this is all around the time of the plebescite: "I am against any kind of joint institution with Muslims and Croats. I personally consider them to be our natural enemies. You already know what natural enemies are, and we can never again live together. We can never again do anything together." Now, did you hear others apart from Mr. Kupresanin express these kinds of sentiments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period before the war, during the war, or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period before the conflict broke out in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I've been listening to the same things from 1990 until 2010.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment, I'm concerned with whether these sort of sentiments were expressed by others in the government or in the Assembly, apart from Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Believe me, Madam Prosecutor, that there were other people who were playing on the Serbian card and trying to ingratiate themselves to Karadzic and others. After that, they would go with their Muslim and Croat brothers and have coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's all I'm going to ask on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just -- there's one intervention in the transcript. At the very end of -- of his answer, the last answer that the witness gave, he gave -- he characterised the behaviour of these people as "Srbovanje," and it wasn't -- it wasn't translated. It's a slang. It is relatively hard word to translate, but I was consulting with -- with the interpreters booth, and they say, beating -- "beating the Serbian drum" might be the closest explanation of that word, if that could be confirmed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's hear the interpreters on the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, agreed, it was -- it was a suggestion, "blowing the Serbian horn," or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, could we locate or identify the word which we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was Srbovanje, S-r-b-o-v-a-n-j-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the English transcript where do we find this word?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was the answer at page 61, line 17. It currently says: "Playing the Serbian card, trying to ingratiate themselves with Karadzic and others."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before Ms. Korner starts, I just forgot to say that our client, Mr. Zupljanin, is not present today. He sent the waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, we were alerted to this last week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And before Ms. Korner takes the floor, could I just address one little matter for the record. I think, Mr. Mandic, that when you started your testimony, you told us your birthday. And your birthday was recorded in the transcript as being the 1st of May. But I noticed that on your statement, it's the 5th of January. So I wonder if there's a mistake. 1/5, or 5/1. So could we just clarify for the record, when actually your birthday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1st of May, the Labour Day. It was three days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I now ask you, please, to have a look at 65 ter 10 -- oh, no, it is P727. It's a record of a -- of a recording of -- of one of your telephone conversations, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, tab number, yeah. It's 123.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not the easiest to read because I'm afraid it's handwriting. You apparently rang up somebody called Samir on the 18th March, and there was a problem, and Samir then called you back. Can we -- we can look at some of the content of this conversation, but can you tell us who Samir was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's obvious that this is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. The first part of the conversation is all about a Mr. Latic. And then can we go, in the English, to the bottom of page 3. And, unfortunately, I don't appear to have marked the part I want. You say that the Vito Zepinic, the Assembly of the Serb People have disowned him. And this is the 18th of March. I'm really sorry, I should have marked this for you, but I haven't, which was a mistake. And you go on to say: "They do not count on him any longer and a procedure will be initiated to disassociate them from him and to relieve him of his duty." And Samir said that is the right thing to do. And Samir asked you: "Who is the candidate for his position? It's Mico, isn't it?" And you said: "Yes, it is Mico." Does that remind you of this conversation? I'm not sure whether we can find it in the handwritten part.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Vito Zepinic resigned on the 4th of April, I think, from his post of deputy minister of the interior. He did that at the office of Momcilo Krajisnik, then Speaker of the Assembly. I can't remember who Samir is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, but all I want to know is, were you aware on the 18th of March that Mico Stanisic was likely to be appointed minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Most probably. Most probably. I suppose somebody informed me. I can't be positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And why Mico Stanisic, rather than you? Because you were in the senior position.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I can only use my common sense and logic to try to infer why I was elected, not Mico Stanisic. I think, as I said before the first break, Mico Stanisic -- sorry. Vitomir Zepinic had already become chief of the Serbian police, but we found out he took bribes and was corrupt. Djeric suggested that Mico Stanisic become minister of the police, because he was probably -- most probably because he was already a member of the Ministerial Council without portfolio or maybe because they hailed from the same area, the mount of Romanija. I can only guess. Or perhaps it was because there was no time to elect a new member of the Ministerial Council or because Mico was the obvious choice because of his qualities, or perhaps because Djeric hailed from the same area. You have to ask that question, either of Djeric or -- or the boss of the -- the party boss, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But that's why I'm asking you, because we can go back to the Ministerial Council. Stanisic was appointed to the Ministerial Council and not you. So why was that? Given, as I say, at that stage, you held the higher position.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I really can't answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mico Stanisic's political affiliations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, Mico was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, but he was good Serb, born in an area populated mostly by Serbs. And one possible reason is that, towards the end of 1991, at one meeting of the professional collegium at the minister of the police, Delimustafic and I suggested that we arrest both Radovan Karadzic and Izetbegovic, and these people of course ran to warn them, so people no longer had any confidence in us. And I was probably regarded as unsuited to the post; likewise, Delimustafic among his own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire of either Mr. Djeric or Mr. Karadzic why it was that you had been, as it were, overlooked for Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I got a very good position myself. I had worked in the justice department for seven or eight years before that, and I thought it was an honour to become a minister of justice. And the work suited me, although I had been in the police for many years before that. Mico was not even mentioned. And there was no -- there were no hard feelings between us on that account, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't think I'm going to take that further. Can we leave that, please, because it is already an exhibit, and can we look --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: But I think, personally, that Djeric, the prime minister, decided that Mico Stanisic should be the minister of the police. He made the decision and he said so at one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, next at document which is -- yep. It's 10312, please. Now, Your Honours, this is not on the 65 ter list, but I want to ask about the contents. Oh, and it's tab 30 for Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can be of any assistance, Ms. Korner, just the -- that you don't say that I always am objecting, I'm trying to assist you on this. If -- in fact, this document has -- has had the number 65 ter 1825, and it was proposed for withdrawal, although some time ago. So I don't know if I was of assistance. The 65 ter -- the 1013 -- the document that you called right now, 10312 has already been on your 65 ter list as 1825. But then it was proposed for withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Put one way or another, is it on our 65 ter list or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will have to figure that yourself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, Mr. Mandic, I want to ask you about this -- no, I don't. I don't want to ask about that document at all. I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be 10312 or -- no, it is 10312, and that's definitely not it. Should be a document dated the 18th of March with the number 0063-7180. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, is that -- is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also you're described there as MR. Momcilo Mandic. I'd like to ask you, this is the 18th of March, so it is more or less -- in fact, I think it's the same day as that intercept we looked at. Why were you sending to the CSBs and to the SUP a document saying: "I also wish to inform you may no longer submit to the MUP any information relating to the work of crime-investigation services ... that a dispatch signed by the assistant minister in charge of duties and tasks relating to crime prevention and detection or the minister himself"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I only asked for compliance with the rules of the service and the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you start off by -- by saying that Mr. Zepinic requested information and had abused his authority in doing so. Why had he abused his authority in doing so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Because he was not supposed to bypass the chief of administration in asking for such information. He was only deputy minister. Only the minister was allowed to ask for information without my consent and without informing me. So he abused his authority as deputy minister and failed to comply with the Law on Internal Affairs and the rules of the service. In fact, by that time, he was already corrupt and bribed, and he was working in circumvention of his own rights and powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it wasn't anything to do with the fact that he wasn't trusted as Serb. It was thought he was too friendly with Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: We were all on good terms with one another and had respect for each other, Serbs and Muslims. But Zepinic had received a Mazda 626 and residence in a neighbourhood called Bosko Buha, and he received that from the SDS party, not from any physical person. To be more precise, from the wing of the SDA [realtime transcript read in error "SDS"] that had begun already to set up a Muslim army within the ranks of the police. The vehicle was later found and -- and confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honours, at the moment I'm still not clear whether it's on our list or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is on our list. It's a document signed by Mr. Mandic, but if Mr. Zecevic wants to object, then -- I don't imagine he does, actually. He want it is in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't want to object. But I just want to be of additional assistance. It is already exhibited. It is 1D119. And Your Honours for the transcript, 68, page 21 [sic] it says in the transcript SDS party and I believe the witness said SDA party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, do I understand, Mr. Zecevic, that this document is already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours, 1D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are indeed grateful for the Defence assistance to the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the objections only come when it's documents they don't want in. When they want them in, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was objecting as a matter of principle, and I was trying to assist you, Ms. Korner. And -- it happens that it was already exhibited, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mandic, leaving aside all that. Can we now look, please, again at a document around this period, which is -- which is ... yes, it's 65 -- no, sorry, it's P532. And it's tab 124. This is an interview you gave to "Javnost," is that right, on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look, please, at the second page in English, and I'm afraid I cannot assist at all where it is in this article, there's discussion about Mr. Latic who was referred to again in this conversation with Samir. And then you were asked about the conflict between you and Dr. Zepinic. And, finally, the reporter says to you: "Dr. Zepinic was promoting undivided MUP at every public appearance of his. How do you comment on that?" And you said: "I am all for undivided MUP, as man of this profession who spent all of his life dealing with this and similar affairs." You had attend, hadn't you, Mr. Mandic, the 11th of February meeting in Banja Luka? You dealt with that in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Madam Prosecutor, I'd like to explain this interview and to add a few points. The executive staff in the police was appointed by ethnicity: The first man was a Muslim, the second a Serb, the third a Croat. That was the principle. And the staff consisted of people who knew each other, respected each other, respected their profession, and mutual tolerance. In the beginning of 1993 [as interpreted], Ilma Salimovic, a Muslim, was replaced without any explanation at the initiative of the Muslim SDA party which was then in power. And he was replaced by Mirsad Srebrenkovic who had worked in the Mesihat of one big mosque in Croatia. He was citizen of Croatia, not Bosnia. Because by that time Croatia was already an independent country. This was a man who, among other things, used to be a teacher at the Mesihat, and the man who was replaced was well respected among his colleague. He was replaced by a hodza, practically, who became responsible for all the personnel in the police. And that then came the breakup of the municipal. On top of that, there was Vitomir Zepinic, prone to bribery and corruption, and then things ripped at the seems completely. Let me say one more thing. The parties in power had very unreasonable demands of us in places where no Muslim was the top man, a Muslim had to be appointed at all costs at the demand of the SDA. The SDS did the same. They insisted on appointments of their own people. We, in the MUP, tried to accommodate this, and we took a unified stand towards the parties to keep the MUP united. With the arrival of this man who came from a mosque into the police force, the united MUP started ripping at all seams, which I hated to see. And to this day, that man is still working in the Mesihat of the Zagreb mosque in Croatia, Mirsad Srebrenkovic is his name. Now can you imagine me with 20 years of service in the police; Bruno Stojic, ten; and all the other people meeting this man, a Muslim, coming from a mosque, who is unable to speak Serbian [as interpreted]. See those people in -- in short three-quarter trousers being appointed to the police force as executives. And that was the reason. And that's -- that's the truth of my interview. And let me just tell you one more thing. When it all ended --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Mandic. You said all that in this interview. And the only question I asked you, the only question I asked you is whether you attended the meeting on February the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I attend all the meetings of the executive staff of the Serbian ethnicity of in the common MUP. Because this man arrived in the end of 1991, and the meeting in Banja Luka was in the beginning of February 1992. By that time, the joint MUP had already fallen apart completely, and we had hundreds of people who arrived from other states, Muslims, to work in the police, without any vetting, without any prior information to us, and in numbers exceeding the job specification arrangements. And they were imposed by executives of Muslim ethnicity. Bratunac, Zvornik, Srebrenica. People would call and say, A man came to us, he can't speak Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: He came to work in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just intervention in the transcript. On page -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, on page 71, line 1, says in the transcript in the beginning of 1993, and I believe witness said at the end of 1991, and he confirmed that on page 72, line 9. And then 71, line 24, he said, Who is unable to speak Serbo-Croatian. That is the -- that is the -- actually, the language that we used in -- in the former Yugoslavia, as -- as the official language. Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. So -- and the same thing is for 72, 15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All, Mr. Mandic - thank you for that explanation - that I wanted to know is, by the time you gave this interview to the "Javnost" in end of March 1992, you had been involved, hadn't you, for some months in -- in the breakup of the old BiH MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. It was broken up by Mirsad Srebrenkovic and one wing of the political leadership of the SDA party. I spent my whole life living and working together with Muslims, and it couldn't cross my mind to break up the joint MUP. All that I gained in my life and learned in my life, I learned together with Muslims. But I didn't want to have this man charting personnel policy having come from the mosque into the police force, and he broke five times a day to pray in the mosque. What if I wanted to leave work and pray in the church? And criticism and expressions of dissatisfaction came in from all sides, and we had to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I understand --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: And Alija Delimustafic was totally unable to cope with this particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, make any attempts, together with Mr. Zepinic, who was not in favour of breaking up the MUP, to get rid of this person you say was no good? And, really, I'd like a simple straightforward answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Zepinic was an inconsequential figure. He was bribed. He didn't dare do anything. He didn't dare to even speak to this Srebrenkovic because he had also paid him off. And that's the worse thing in anywhere in any trade, especially in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask you about that article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move now, please, to the next document, which is ... just a moment. I've just got to change my binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is one questioning relating to an intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's document 3224.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Between you and somebody called Kepes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Milenko Kepes was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were talking to him apparently.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Could you be mistaken about the last name?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you have a look. Could you have a look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I am looking at the screen, Kepes. Milenko Kepes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't know who that is, although you had a long conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me see what we talked about. If you could sort of leaf through this intercept. How many pages are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You appear to be discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I can be assistance, maybe it would be easier for the witness to shuffle through the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if you just have a quick look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because it's in Serbian, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Milenko Karisik, commander of the Serbian specials. It is not Kepes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's why I was confused. It was Milenko Karisik, not Milenko Kepes. He was Deputy Commander of the joint special force, Dragan Minkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Is that -- Vukic, isn't it, who was commander of the special forces? Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Vikic. Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Well, that explains that. Yes, can I ask you to look, please, at the transcript of another intercept around this same time. It's 1067. This is you, Mr. Mandic, talking to somebody called Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I listened to this recording earlier today. It was in April. You see at the top 18th of April. I was still on the police force. We had received information that the Territorial Defence, that is members of the Territorial Defence of Muslim ethnicity, were about to make a raid on the factory in Vogosca to seize weapons, so I informed Vukota Vukovic whom I did not know, actually, and told him to take care of that to prevent this theft of weapons by Muslim members of the Territorial Defence, because we had received a report that they were about to raid the factory and take the weapons by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And all I want to know is, who was this gentleman, or who were you speaking to? Was he army or TO or ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: He was a military man employed at that military factory producing weapons. I don't know the man personally, but he was a brother at work colleague of mine. But I had never met the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ans this is the same Vikic who had been with Karisik, the commander of the special brigade of the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this is the same person or someone else who was leading those Muslim members of the Territorial Defence. It is possible that it's the same person, but I'm not sure. The armed conflict in Sarajevo had already begun.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your -- you're talking about Ustashas. Was Vikic a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Half Croat, half Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can we look, please, at -- yeah. Please, Exhibit 1162. It's tab 44.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I think you listened to this one - oh, sorry - today, the actual tape. And it's Karadzic talking apparently to Stanisic. Were you able to recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I think I recognised the voices of Mico Stanisic and Dr. Radovan Karadzic. But I don't know what they were talking about. But I definitely recognised their voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to come on to what they were talking about, because we just played enough for you -- It appears they are talking about you, because if we look at the context, it says: "There's a problem this morning. They released them this morning." And they're asked -- Dr. Karadzic asked - this is the 18th of April: "Who released them?" And Mico Stanisic said: "It seems Momo did." "Why?" And then over the page -- go over the page in B/C/S as well. "I don't know. He didn't [sic] -- he released some ten guys this morning (Mico is talking to Momo in the office). Momo released them, they were [sic] his neighbours over there because of the parents and this ..." And does that remind you what this was about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who had you released and about which Dr. Karadzic was getting so annoyed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was conveyed to Dr. Karadzic, but I know it was about children, even minors, or young adults who were walking around the Mount Igman armed. They were playing war, and they were arrested by the police. They were brought to the school. I gave them some sandwiches and then let them go home. And I received calls from their parents who were acquaintances of mine. I didn't believe it was proper for them to be detained, and that's why I sent them back. Probably somebody informed Dr. Karadzic that this was some very serious army in question or even territorials. I think this is what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. So you're saying that the police had arrested children. Was this up in the direction of Vrace? You said Mount Igman. But was this anything to do with Vrace?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it is probably in the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because it goes on to say later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at the third page, please. I think it says there that: "Momo should be transferred to the Ministry of Justice. Do it for Christ's sake." And Mico replies: "That what's I was saying. That cannot be done like that. Ten terrorists were let go, man; we're going to lose the war."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now what would Mico Stanisic have to do with transferring you to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I have no idea, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you -- as far as you're concerned, you didn't let ten terrorists go; you let ten children go.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, those were children who took arms and played war. Probably according to the rules of service, I should have handed them over to the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: And I was trying to justify my actions to Karadzic because he received information that those were terrorists. Because they -- they were armed in the Serb-held terrorists. And I knew those children. They were not terrorists. I didn't agree then with the views of my bosses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Later on, and I'm not going trouble you with you it, you said to -- you actually took over the phone yourself and said that these were young men -- you told Dr. Karadzic these were young men from Hrasnica where your parents live.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was a Muslim-dominated place, but I knew those children, and I knew I should let them go. But who informed Mr. Karadzic that these individuals were terrorist, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you told us a minute ago that you didn't agree with the views of your bosses, which views didn't you agree with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, I believed that the persons involved were not terrorist but, rather, children playing war. They were playing with fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by your bosses, who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I meant President Karadzic. Because he had been informed that those were terrorists, and I believe the opposite, that they were not the terrorists. I don't know who passed this information to him. It was irrelevant to me. Those were children who were hungry. I ordered somebody to make them sandwiches, and I let them go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And apparently Mico Stanisic didn't -- did Mico Stanisic know that these were children?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. Mico Stanisic was not in Vrace. He was at Pale. He was probably wrongly informed too. You know, you have this kind of flanked channels of information. Everybody was informing the President of the state about an imminent danger or something like that. I believe that Mico himself didn't know what this was all about either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. You took over the telephone from Mico Stanisic so the two of you were together.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: He came later, and we discussed this. When this event happened, I was on my own. As far as executive of the Serbian police in Vrace were concerned, Mico was at the MUP headquarters in Pale. It was my own decision and I carried it out. Now, who informed the then president Mr. Karadzic and the minister of the police that I let some people go, I don't know. It must have been someone from amongst my associates. They wanted to show off and alarm people about the danger threatening the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask but that document; thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, now at a document which we haven't looked at before, which is 372. Tab 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that your -- is that a stamp and signature -- and your signature again?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's an order dated the 19th of April to the public security stations in Sarajevo. Talking about the organisational patrols, seizing vehicles, and seizing items for which the owner cannot not prove origin and hand them over to the nearest police station. You signed that order. Where was Mico Stanisic at this point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I did in this coordination with the then minister, he knew about this order of mine, which is in compliance with the rules of service to present escalation of crime, everything that I listed here, violence, terror, robberies, et cetera, and to try to protect the life and limb and the property of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the last thing that you ordered under item 4 was, Urgently order the -- organise the crime service and these activities in the field including, amongst others, the execution of on-site investigations. What was the necessity for this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, this is in accordance with the Law on the Interior, and it's all in the line of the work of the CID, to detect crimes, to work in the field, and possibly, if any crime, like robbery or murder was detected, to carry out crime-scene investigation and to document the event. This is according to the Rules of Service and the Law on Interior. I had been working in that environment for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I want to ask you. Why, as it was in the law, was it necessary for you to tell the police to carry out the law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, you always have to give tasks to police and to try to push them to work. That's how things work. I'm talking about the local police and the lower-ranking police officers. That's why you have executives and bosses who are going to push the people beneath them to perform their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But was it --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I mean, this is customary. These kind of orders were a customary thing to be issued by executives in the police force, to protect the property, individuals, public law and order and to prevent theft, robberies, murders, et cetera, because we were witnessing escalation because, on the 6th, the armed conflicts in Sarajevo started. And groups of people emerged on both sides. And, of course, in coordination with Mr. Stanisic, I attempted to reinstate peace and order as much as was possible at the moment, and one of the ways to do that was to issue such an order which is to force people out into the street to do their job and to protect the people and their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's what I'm asking. Was the necessity for you to issue such an order the fact that the police was simply not doing their job?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. It was total chaos. Everything was in disarray. You know, you work in a system all your life, and then the system changes. The organisation changes. People were lost. They -- they couldn't cope with switching from one system to another. People had total confusion in their heads, so they needed to be assisted in carrying out their duties. That's how I perceived it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, please, next, then, to -- yes, document 9249, please. Tab 49.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just, I want to know about this one. It's addressed to the minister and the deputy minister, 21st of April. And as it report if you look at the signature, from the -- Mr. Jesuric, the Bijeljina CSB chief. Did you get that report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page, please, in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Predrag Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Did you get this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you, in the normal course of events, have received reports as part of your job as deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Probably, under normal circumstances, I might have received it, Madam Prosecutor, but I don't remember this document. Because Jesuric was chief of the Bijeljina centre, including Bijeljina and Klopere [phoen], and he submitted a report on the situation in those three towns.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I can't remember who it's been gone through with, but it has been gone through with somebody. I can't remember why it was MFI'd, but I'm asking now that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I -- I remember why it was MFI'd myself, but -- I don't -- I don't think that the -- that the sufficient nexus between this witness and this document has been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sent addressed to this witness as a deputy minister, which in the normal course of events he would have received, even if he can't remember this. I don't know what else one can do with a document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just go back, please, to the document before that, which I missed out by mistake, and that's an intercept record between you and your brother. And it's P728. Now Mladen Mandic, that's right, was your brother, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was he based?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of April, in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Sorry, you can see here that he was in Pale, or I was in Pale. But, in April, he was in Vrace with me; in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. Because you're in Pale. Now all I want to ask you about is, at the second page, where he says to you: "I hear some of Seselj's Men and these from Vukovar have come, but they're not very good." Did you know that paramilitary had been sent there by Seselj? Sorry, it's the third page in B/C/S; I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not the Seselj's Men. It was Brne Gavrilovic, a man from Sarajevo. He was a member of Seselj's party. He was born in Grbavica, and he lived on the edges of Sarajevo. They used to call themselves Seselj's Men, the radicals, et cetera. But those were Sarajevo people who were members of the Seselj's party, and they were members of the Territorial Defence of Grbavica. They had probably been on the front before, but I know for sure that they lived on the edges of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, finally, the last document for today, please, then, can we look at document number 52 ... yes, 1338.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's tab number 52.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 1st of May, so this was before you became minister of justice, wasn't it, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you about that. Because if we go, then, to the last page, which is page 3 in English and page 4 in B/C/S. It's going out -- under your signature, is that right, even though I think you didn't sign it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is not my signature. And it says "for."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you know who signed it on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the content. What I want to know is why it's going out under your signature as minister of justice, as you hadn't been appointed yet. That's the first thing I want to know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: This should be explained by the person who signed it. I know that I started signing my documents from the date I was appointed. That was about two weeks afterwards. Maybe somebody was too hasty. I was informed towards the end of April about my appointment to the position of the minister, and somebody rushed to send out a kind of -- this kind of letter on behalf of myself as the minister. I don't know who that person could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back to the first page, please. It's addressed to the President of the regional -- region's Assemblies of Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Trebinje, Bijeljina, and Doboj, and it refers to the decisions about the functioning of courts and penal/correctional facilities. And then it sets all of that out. Now, even though you didn't sign this, were you aware that this document was being sent?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know. I -- I got hold of this document later. And the sequence of movement was wrong. It was supposed to be decided by the Assembly on the forming of the judiciary and prosecutor's office, and only after that would the Ministry of Justice start working on that to pass enactments on forming penal and connect correctional facilities, lower and higher courts, supreme courts, prosecutor's offices, magistrate courts, et cetera. Somebody signed this document too early, before all these decisions were taken. It must first be decided by the Assembly and the president of the republic who has constitutional powers during war to issue such decisions concerning judiciary, prosecutor's office, district prisons attached to district courts, and such-like things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But the only point that I want to make apart from the fact that this is setting what has to be done is, were these addressed to the Assemblies of the various autonomous regions, Krajina, Birac, all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska was divided into five regions: Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Herzegovina, Semberija, and Doboj. It was identical to the situation that prevailed before the war. And at the level of regions you had, first instance, lower courts, and then district courts for more serious crimes. And attached to district courts were prisons where people who were under investigation were being kept. So if you have time, I can explain to this. That is how the remand prison in Banja Luka and Sarajevo were established, as well as in Trebinje, Bijeljina, and Doboj. In all the five regional centres where the seat of district courts were, those were second instance courts for minor offences, and you have first instance courts for more serious crimes. And they were under the jurisdiction of these courts, district courts, that the prisons were set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. All I was trying to establish from this was whether these areas corresponded with the Serb Autonomous Regions that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they coincided with autonomous regions, but with the regions and the seat of district courts, they did coincide. I'm not sure. This was the scheme and the chart that originates from before the war, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is -- is there any objection to this? Because inasmuch as I understand the witness is saying the document is premature, he speaks generally about it. He agrees with you about it speaking to these regions, but that's about it. That's the only --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He says he got hold of it after it went out. He said that -- I can't remember -- Your Honours, I'll find that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I do remember that answer, and I -- I was waiting for clarification as to how soon afterwards was -- whether it was -- was it within the period that he would have been a minister, or are we talking about something very recent?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understood --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell -- when did you get a hold of this, Mr. Mandic? Was it after you were formally appointed; or are you talking about much, much later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Much later. I believe it was one of the OTP investigators who showed me this document. Although this document is essentially correct, it is premature and not really authentic. Somebody was too much in a rush in organising the justice department. There are documents from later on that follow up on this reorganisation of the whole justice system and the courts from misdemeanor courts to other courts. They were signed by the President of the Republic and enacted by the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, it is 7.00, Ms. Korner, could we return to this tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean, no. Let's try and get it out of the way. Either it's admitted or it's not, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we object based on what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I appreciate that it's 7.00, but, I mean, I don't want to return to this tomorrow morning again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you mean to say that in the whole of the time where you were minister of justice, from May until November, you never knew this document had been sent out and never saw it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: As can see from the signature, it's not mine. If the minister has not been appointed, nobody in the whole justice ministry has been appointed. I don't know who would have had the powers to do this if the minister had not been appointed. However, as a document, it is corroborated by later documents that confirm this decision and these later documents are laws properly signed by the President and adopted by the Assembly. Now, on the 1st May, who could have written this, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the answer, isn't it, it's corroborated by later documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway we'll take the adjournment now and resume tomorrow morning. I so would prefer to think about this. And we'll deal with this first thing tomorrow morning. Mr. Mandic, although you would have appeared as a witness previously, I'm obliged to remind you that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot talk with counsel on either side, and such conversations you have outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we will reconvene tomorrow morning in Courtroom III, at 9.00. Thank you.
